source_text:
Nec nobis de nostra frequentia blandiamur: multi nobis uidemur, sed Deo admodum pauci sumus. nos gentes nationesque distinguimus: Deo una domus est mundus hic totus. reges statum regni sui per officia ministrorum diuersa nouerunt: Deo indiciis opus non est: non enim solum in oculis eius, sed in sinu uiuimus.
sed Iudaeis nihil profuit, quod unum et ipsi Deum aris atque templis maxima superstitione coluerunt. ignorantia laberis, si priorum aut oblitus ant inscius posteriorum recordaris.
nam et ipsi Deum nostrum, idem enim omnium Deus est, experti sunt: quamdiu enim eum caste, innoxie religioseque coluerunt, quamdiu praeceptis salubribus obtemperauerunt, de paucis innumeri facti, de egentibus diuites, de seruientibus reges: modici multos, inermi armatos, dum fugiunt insequentes, Dei iussu et elementis adnitentibus obruerunt.
scripta eorum relege, uel si Romanis magis gaudes, ut transeamus ueteres, [Flaui Josephi uel] Antonii Iuliani de Iudaeis require: iam scies, nequitia sua hanc eos meruisse fortunam, nec quidquam accidisse quod non sit iis, si in contumacia perseuerarent, ante praedictum.
ita prius eos deseruisse conprehendes quam esse desertos nec, ut impie loqueris, cum Deo suo captos, sed a Deo ut disciplinae transfugas deditos.
thought_title: God's knowledge of all peoples and the Jews' desertion
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's attack on Christians, arguing that God knows all people without needing reports and that the Jews' misfortunes came from their own disobedience.
pass_a_gloss: And let us not flatter ourselves about our own numbers: we seem many to ourselves, but to God we are quite few. We distinguish peoples and nations: to God this whole world is one house. Kings have learned the state of their kingdom through the various services of ministers: God has no need of informers: for we live not only in his sight, but in his bosom. But it profited the Jews nothing that they too worshipped the one God with altars and temples with the greatest superstition. You slip through ignorance, if you recall the later things having forgotten or being unaware of the earlier things. For they too experienced our God, for he is the God of all: for as long as they worshipped him chastely, innocently and religiously, as long as they obeyed his health-giving commands, from few they became countless, from needy rich, from slaves kings: few overwhelmed many, unarmed overwhelmed armed, while fleeing they overwhelmed pursuers, by God's command and with the elements assisting. Read again their writings, or if you rejoice more in Roman authors, so that we may pass over the ancients, inquire about the Jews from Flavius Josephus or Antonius Julianus: you will then know that by their own wickedness they deserved this fortune, and that nothing happened which was not foretold to them beforehand, if they should persist in obstinacy. Thus you will grasp that they deserted God before they were deserted, and not, as you impiously say, that they were captured with their God, but that they were handed over by God as deserters from discipline.

choices.term: multi nobis uidemur, sed Deo admodum pauci sumus
choices.english: we seem many to ourselves, but to God we are quite few
choices.why: Keeps the contrast between human appearance and divine reckoning, preserving the dative of reference 'nobis' and 'Deo'.
rejected: we think we are many, but before God we are very few

choices.term: Deo una domus est mundus hic totus
choices.english: to God this whole world is one house
choices.why: Preserves the dative 'Deo' and the predicate structure, emphasizing God's universal perspective against human divisions.
rejected: God has one house, this entire world

choices.english: God has no need of informers
choices.why: Renders 'indiciis' as informers to capture the contrast with kings' ministers and the sense of reports about subjects.
rejected: God has no need of information

choices.why: Keeps the intimate spatial metaphor of living within God's embrace, stronger than mere sight.

choices.english: handed over as deserters from discipline
choices.why: Preserves the military metaphor of 'transfugas' and the passive 'deditos', showing God as the agent of their surrender.
rejected: given up as deserters of discipline

choices.why: Uses the required glossary term 'superstition' for 'superstitio', keeping the ironic force that even their worship of the true God was excessive.

pass_b_english: Nor should we flatter ourselves about our numbers. We seem many to ourselves, but to God we are quite few. We divide the world into peoples and nations, but to God this whole world is one house. Kings learn the state of their kingdom through the varied services of their ministers, but God has no need of informers, for we live not only in his sight but in his bosom.

Yet it did the Jews no good that they too worshipped one God with altars and temples and the greatest superstition. You slip into ignorance if you remember only their earlier history and forget or never knew their later one.

For they too experienced our God, and he is the God of all. As long as they worshipped him purely, innocently, and religiously, as long as they obeyed his wholesome commands, from a few they became countless, from poor they became rich, from slaves they became kings. A small band overwhelmed many, unarmed men overwhelmed armed ones, fleeing men overwhelmed their pursuers, by God's command and with the elements assisting them.

Read their writings again, or if you prefer Roman authors, to pass over the ancients, consult Flavius Josephus or Antonius Julianus on the Jews. Then you will learn that their own wickedness earned them this fate, and that nothing happened to them that had not been foretold, if they persisted in their defiance.

So you will understand that they abandoned God before they were abandoned, and that they were not, as you impiously say, captured along with their God, but handed over by God as deserters from discipline.
notes: The phrase 'Flaui Josephi uel' is bracketed in the source text, indicating possible interpolation or textual uncertainty; it is translated as part of the source as given.

problems.quote: You slip into ignorance if you remember only their later history and forget or never knew their earlier one.
problems.source_quote: ignorantia laberis, si priorum aut oblitus ant inscius posteriorum recordaris.
problems.why: Reverses the order of earlier (priorum) and later (posteriorum) histories, changing the intended meaning.
problems.fix: You slip into ignorance if you remember only their earlier history and forget or are ignorant of the later.

edits.old: You slip into ignorance if you remember only their later history and forget or never knew their earlier one.
edits.new: You slip into ignorance if you remember only their earlier history and forget or never knew their later one.

fixed: Reversed the order of priorum (earlier) and posteriorum (later) in the English; corrected to match the source.

last_rejected.quote: You slip into ignorance if you remember only their earlier history and forget or never knew their later one
last_rejected.source_quote: ignorantia laberis, si priorum aut oblitus ant inscius posteriorum recordaris
last_rejected.why: 'laberis' means 'you are deceived/led astray', not 'you slip into ignorance'; 'ignorantia' is ablative of manner ('in ignorance'), not the object.
last_rejected.fix: You are deceived in your ignorance if, forgetful of earlier times or unaware of later ones, you recall only...
last_rejected.ruling: laberis = 'you slip' with ignorance as circumstance; translation 'you slip into ignorance' only slightly shifts nuance, not a major error.

polish.changed: Clarified speaker continuity, smoothed sentence rhythm, made pronoun references explicit, and adjusted paragraph breaks to match the argument's turns.

notes.quote: consult Flavius Josephus or Antonius Julianus on the Jews
notes.fix: Note: Josephus was a Jewish historian; Antonius Julianus a Roman historian.
